claim: Cervical cancer causes approximately 600,000 incident cases and 340,000 deaths each year worldwide.
source: Cervical cancer causes substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide, with approximately 600,000 incident cases and 340,000 deaths each year (Singh et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2023

claim: Cervical cancer is caused by persistent infection with one of approximately 13 carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) types.
source: Globally, cervical cancer is caused by persistent infection with one of ~13 carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) types (Schiffman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schiffman et al., 2007

claim: Nearly 85% of cervical cancer cases occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC).
source: nearly 85% of cervical cancer cases and almost 90% of cervical cancer deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) (IARC, 2022; Ferlay et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to IARC, 2022 and Ferlay et al., 2020

claim: Almost 90% of cervical cancer deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC).
source: nearly 85% of cervical cancer cases and almost 90% of cervical cancer deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) (IARC, 2022; Ferlay et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to IARC, 2022 and Ferlay et al., 2020

claim: The maximum potential health benefits of vaccinating adolescents today will not be achieved for 40 years.
source: the maximum potential health benefits of vaccinating adolescents today will not be achieved for 40 years.
evidence: Based on inference about the time lag between vaccination and cancer prevention

claim: Rapid implementation of a broad, effective cervical screening campaign for adult women in the highest-burden areas will advance cancer control by 20 years.
source: However, the rapid implementation of a broad, effective cervical screening campaign for adult women in the highest-burden areas will advance cancer control by 20 years (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 showing timing projections

claim: A one-time screening campaign for women aged 30-49 years in selected countries would cost approximately US$2.5 billion to avert approximately 570,000 deaths.
source: A one-time screening campaign for women aged 30–49 years in the selected countries yielded a financial cost of ~US$2.5 billion to avert ~570,000 deaths, or US$4,400 per death averted.
evidence: Based on modeling projections described in the manuscript

claim: A one-time single-dose bivalent HPV vaccination campaign of girls aged 9-14 years in selected countries would cost approximately US$2.0 billion and avert approximately 640,000 deaths.
source: On a similar order of magnitude, a one-time single-dose bivalent HPV vaccination campaign of girls aged 9–14 years in the same countries would cost ~US$2.0 billion and avert ~640,000 deaths, or US$3,200 per death averted.
evidence: Based on modeling projections described in the manuscript

claim: The detection of carcinogenic cervical/vaginal HPV DNA is currently the most sensitive screening method to distinguish those with an appreciable risk of precancer or cancer from those at low risk.
source: The detection of carcinogenic cervical/vaginal HPV DNA is currently the most sensitive screening method to distinguish those with an appreciable risk of precancer or cancer from those at low risk (Demarco et al., 2022; Castle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Demarco et al., 2022 and Castle et al., 2012

claim: The WHO currently recommends HPV testing as preferred over visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) as the primary screening method where resources permit.
source: HPV testing is preferred to using visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) as the primary screening method where resources permit (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2021

claim: Meta-analyses comparing the performance of self-collected to clinician-collected samples using PCR-based HPV detection showed similar sensitivity and specificity for the detection of cervical precancer.
source: The results from meta-analyses comparing the performance of self-collected to clinician-collected samples, using PCR-based HPV detection, showed similar sensitivity and specificity for the detection of cervical precancer (Arbyn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arbyn et al., 2018

claim: As of 2022, seven LMICs were recommending HPV self-collection.
source: As of 2022, seven LMICs were recommending HPV self-collection (Serrano et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Serrano et al., 2022

claim: Treatment of all HPV-positive women with thermal ablation may substantially overtreat infections, only the minority of which would progress to cancer.
source: Treatment of all HPV-positive women with thermal ablation (i.e. screen-treat strategy) is an option under current WHO guidelines (World Health Organization, 2021); however, this may substantially overtreat infections, only the minority of which would progress to cancer (Demarco et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Demarco et al., 2020

claim: Visual examination techniques including VIA are subject to human error, have low accuracy for precancer, and require continuous training and quality control measures.
source: However, these techniques are subject to human error, have low accuracy for precancer, and require continuous training and quality control measures (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003; Catarino et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003 and Catarino et al., 2018

claim: HPV16 is the most carcinogenic HPV genotype.
source: HPV16 is the most carcinogenic, followed by HPV18/45, followed by HPV31/33/35/52/58, followed by HPV39/51/56/59/68 (Guan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guan et al., 2012

claim: HPV genotype carcinogenicity varies predictably across populations in the order: HPV16, then HPV18/45, then HPV31/33/35/52/58, then HPV39/51/56/59/68.
source: HPV genotyping is a newer, more accurate method of triage, as genotype carcinogenicity varies predictably across populations (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2009; Qiao et al., 2008). HPV16 is the most carcinogenic, followed by HPV18/45, followed by HPV31/33/35/52/58, followed by HPV39/51/56/59/68 (Guan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2009; Qiao et al., 2008; and Guan et al., 2012

claim: Automated visual evaluation (AVE) using an Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithm shows promise as a relatively simple and fast triage method.
source: AVE using an Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithm shows promise as a relatively simple and fast triage method that could be used in conjunction with HPV genotyping to generate a highly accurate composite triage test (Desai et al., 2020; Desai et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Desai et al., 2020 and Desai et al., 2022b

claim: The PAVE study aims to recruit up to 100,000 women in nine countries.
source: The study aims to recruit up to 100,000 women in nine countries: Brazil, Cambodia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Honduras, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania (Figure 3 and Figure 4).
evidence: Stated study design with reference to figures showing study locations

claim: The PAVE study is being conducted in Brazil, Cambodia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Honduras, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania.
source: The study aims to recruit up to 100,000 women in nine countries: Brazil, Cambodia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Honduras, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania (Figure 3 and Figure 4).
evidence: Stated study design with reference to figures showing study locations

claim: Eligibility criteria for the PAVE study include individuals with a cervix aged 30-49 years (general population) or 25-49 years if living with HIV.
source: Eligibility criteria are: individuals with a cervix aged 30–49 years (general population) or 25–49 years if living with HIV (WLHIV), not currently pregnant, and able to understand study risks, benefits, and alternatives and provide informed consent in their native language.

claim: Pregnant women are excluded from the PAVE study.
source: Pregnant women, or those with no cervix or having been treated for a cervical cancer are excluded.

claim: Women with no cervix are excluded from the PAVE study.
source: Pregnant women, or those with no cervix or having been treated for a cervical cancer are excluded.

claim: Women having been treated for cervical cancer are excluded from the PAVE study.
source: Pregnant women, or those with no cervix or having been treated for a cervical cancer are excluded.

claim: At each study site, approximately 1-2% prevalence of histopathologic precancers (HPV-positive adjudicated CIN2+/AIS) is anticipated.
source: At each study site, we anticipate ~1–2% prevalence of histopathologic precancers (HPV-positive adjudicated CIN2+/AIS), yielding about 100–200 precancers and a very few cancers out of a sample of 10,000 women.

claim: Combined across all countries, the PAVE study anticipates up to 1000-2000 precancers.
source: Combined across all countries, we anticipate up to 1000–2000 precancers.

claim: Participants in the PAVE study self-collect a vaginal sample for HPV testing using a FLOQSwab.
source: Participants self-collect a vaginal sample for HPV testing using a FLOQSwab (Copan) following instruction by study personnel.

claim: All PAVE sites intend to use the ScreenFire HPV risk-stratification (RS) assay.
source: All sites intend to use the ScreenFire HPV risk-stratification (RS) assay (ScreenFire) (U.S. patent 11091799, Atila Biosystems Inc, Sunnyvale, CA, U.S.) (Desai et al., 2022a; Inturrisi et al., 2024).
evidence: Stated study protocol with citations to Desai et al., 2022a and Inturrisi et al., 2024

claim: On average, approximately 80% of participants will screen HPV-negative.
source: On average, approximately 80% of participants will screen HPV-negative, but this varies by study population.

claim: Women with HPV-positive results undergo a speculum exam with an application of 5% acetic acid.
source: Women with HPV-positive results undergo a speculum exam with an application of 5% acetic acid.

claim: Cervical images in the PAVE study are collected using the Iris device (Liger Medical LLC, Lehi, UT, U.S.).
source: Cervical images will be collected by a trained study provider using a dedicated device (Iris, Liger Medical LLC, Lehi, UT, U.S.).

claim: Biopsies are collected from up to four acetowhite areas for each participant.
source: Biopsies will be collected from up to four acetowhite areas for each participant.

claim: If no acetowhite areas are seen, then an endocervical sample or cytology will be collected.
source: If no acetowhite areas are seen, then an endocervical sample (using curette or brush) or cytology will be collected.

claim: Sites using VIA will use Softbiopsy/SoftECC brush biopsy (Histologics LLC, Anaheim, CA, U.S.).
source: Sites using VIA will use Softbiopsy/SoftECC brush biopsy (Histologics LLC, Anaheim, CA, U.S.), a device that is simpler to learn and perform and is associated with lower bleeding risk.

claim: Softbiopsy/SoftECC brush biopsy is simpler to learn and perform and is associated with lower bleeding risk compared to standard biopsy.
source: Sites using VIA will use Softbiopsy/SoftECC brush biopsy (Histologics LLC, Anaheim, CA, U.S.), a device that is simpler to learn and perform and is associated with lower bleeding risk.

claim: All women that have an HPV-positive test are expected to have a histologic diagnosis.
source: All women that have an HPV-positive test are expected to have a histologic diagnosis (biopsy, endocervical sample (ECC), and/or excisional tissue diagnosis).

claim: The PAVE strategy combines extended genotyping and visual evaluation assisted by deep-learning-based AVE to triage HPV-positive participants.
source: The PAVE strategy aims to target cervical precancer accurately and affordably by (1) self-sampled HPV screening; (2) triage among HPV-positive participants by combination of extended genotyping and visual evaluation assisted by deep-learning-based AVE; and (3) treatment using thermal ablation or excision Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ).

claim: The PAVE strategy uses treatment with thermal ablation or excision Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ).
source: The PAVE strategy aims to target cervical precancer accurately and affordably by (1) self-sampled HPV screening; (2) triage among HPV-positive participants by combination of extended genotyping and visual evaluation assisted by deep-learning-based AVE; and (3) treatment using thermal ablation or excision Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ).

claim: The PAVE protocol combines the three-class classification label provided by the AVE algorithm with the four hrHPV risk group strata to create 12 strata of risk of precancer.
source: The PAVE screen-triage-treat protocol combines the three-class classification label (normal, indeterminate, precancer+) provided by the AVE algorithm with the four hrHPV risk group strata to create 12 strata of risk of precancer (Table 2).
evidence: Stated study methodology with reference to Table 2

claim: The AVE algorithm provides three-class classification labels: normal, indeterminate, and precancer+.
source: The PAVE screen-triage-treat protocol combines the three-class classification label (normal, indeterminate, precancer+) provided by the AVE algorithm with the four hrHPV risk group strata to create 12 strata of risk of precancer (Table 2).
evidence: Stated study methodology with reference to Table 2

claim: The primary objective of the PAVE protocol is to compare the sensitivity at a given specificity level of the PAVE approach for triaging HPV-positive women to current standard of care.
source: The primary objective of the PAVE protocol is to compare the sensitivity at a given specificity level of the PAVE approach for triaging HPV-positive women to current SOC (HPV testing without genotyping triaged by VIA or colposcopic impression) (Figure 6).
evidence: Stated study objective with reference to Figure 6

claim: The PAVE study hypothesizes that the difference of two sensitivities (PAVE minus SOC) will be significantly greater than zero.
source: We hypothesize that the difference of two sensitivities (PAVE minus SOC) conducted on the overall consortium data will be significantly greater than zero (the null hypothesis of no difference in sensitivity), indicating that PAVE detects more precancer than SOC triage at the same level of specificity.

claim: ScreenFire was compared against reference research HPV DNA assays in 2078 stored specimens.
source: ScreenFire was compared against reference research HPV DNA assays in 2078 stored specimens.

claim: Overall concordance for ScreenFire for both viral types was greater than 90%.
source: Overall concordance for both viral types was >90%, and sensitivity for CIN3 + was 94.2%, similar to Linear Array (93.1%) and TypeSeq (95.9%), indicating excellent performance (Inturrisi et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inturrisi et al., 2024

claim: ScreenFire sensitivity for CIN3+ was 94.2%.
source: Overall concordance for both viral types was >90%, and sensitivity for CIN3 + was 94.2%, similar to Linear Array (93.1%) and TypeSeq (95.9%), indicating excellent performance (Inturrisi et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inturrisi et al., 2024

claim: Linear Array sensitivity for CIN3+ was 93.1%.
source: Overall concordance for both viral types was >90%, and sensitivity for CIN3 + was 94.2%, similar to Linear Array (93.1%) and TypeSeq (95.9%), indicating excellent performance (Inturrisi et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inturrisi et al., 2024

claim: TypeSeq sensitivity for CIN3+ was 95.9%.
source: Overall concordance for both viral types was >90%, and sensitivity for CIN3 + was 94.2%, similar to Linear Array (93.1%) and TypeSeq (95.9%), indicating excellent performance (Inturrisi et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inturrisi et al., 2024

claim: In El Salvador, 5% of HPV-negative women will undergo colposcopic evaluation.
source: The exception is El Salvador, at which 5% of those screening HPV-negative undergo colposcopic examination.
evidence: Stated study protocol for El Salvador site

claim: Four AI algorithms are being developed and evaluated in the PAVE study: cervix detector, image quality classifier, disease classifier to identify precancer, and treatability/SCJ classifier.
source: During the PAVE study, four AI algorithms are being developed and evaluated: (1) cervix detector, (2) image quality classifier, (3) disease classifier to identify precancer, and (4) treatability/SCJ classifier.

claim: The following cases will be reviewed by an expert gynecologic pathologist: all cases with histology CIN2+ or HSIL, all HPV16+ with <CIN2 pathology, all cases read as precancer+ on AVE, and 5% of biopsies read as normal.
source: To assure histopathology reading standardization, the following cases will be reviewed by an expert gynecologic pathologist, making use of a Motic whole slide scan review collection and transfer: (1) all cases with histology CIN2 + or high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL); (2) all HPV16 + with <CIN2 pathology; (3) all cases read as precancer + on AVE; and (4) 5% of biopsies read as normal.

claim: Results will be classified for the study purposes as normal, low-grade (<CIN2), high-grade (CIN2, CIN3), adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), or invasive cervical cancer.
source: Results will be classified for the study purposes as normal, low-grade (<CIN2), high-grade (CIN2, CIN3), adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), or invasive cervical cancer (squamous, adenosquamous, adenocarcinoma, or other).

claim: About half of the CIN3+ cases are estimated to be positive for HPV16.
source: We estimate that about half of the CIN3 + cases will be positive for HPV16, and about 10–15% will be HPV18/45 positive, and that the remaining two other channels will have a 20% prevalence within cases.

claim: About 10-15% of CIN3+ cases are estimated to be HPV18/45 positive.
source: We estimate that about half of the CIN3 + cases will be positive for HPV16, and about 10–15% will be HPV18/45 positive, and that the remaining two other channels will have a 20% prevalence within cases.

claim: The remaining two other HPV channels (HPV31/33/35/52/58 and HPV39/51/56/59/68) are estimated to have a 20% prevalence within CIN3+ cases.
source: We estimate that about half of the CIN3 + cases will be positive for HPV16, and about 10–15% will be HPV18/45 positive, and that the remaining two other channels will have a 20% prevalence within cases.

claim: During the efficacy phase, clinicians will not be provided with HPV genotyping, AI algorithm outputs, or risk strata.
source: During the efficacy phase, the PAVE algorithm is undergoing evaluation and development, and clinicians will not be provided with HPV genotyping, AI algorithm outputs, or risk strata.
evidence: Stated study protocol for efficacy phase

claim: When the efficacy phase is complete, if the PAVE algorithm outperforms the SOC, the effectiveness phase will begin.
source: When the efficacy phase is complete, if the PAVE algorithm outperforms the SOC, we will begin the effectiveness phase.

claim: A microsimulation model of genotype-specific HPV natural history and cervical carcinogenesis is being developed specifically for evaluation of novel biomarker triage tests, including AVE.
source: A microsimulation model of genotype-specific HPV natural history and cervical carcinogenesis is being developed specifically for evaluation of novel biomarker triage tests, including AVE (Campos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campos et al., 2021

claim: The number of screening or adolescent HPV vaccinations needed to avert one cervical cancer death was similar for each intervention (293 for screening; 278 for vaccination).
source: According to our projections, the number of interventions needed to avert one cervical cancer death was similar for HPV vaccination and screening (i.e. 278 for HPV vaccination; 293 for screening).
evidence: Based on modeling projections described in the manuscript

claim: A preliminary interim analysis on the efficacy of the PAVE strategy is expected to be completed by early 2024.
source: It is expected that a preliminary interim analysis on the efficacy of the PAVE strategy will be completed by the early 2024, and field recruitment will be completed by end of 2024.

claim: Field recruitment for the PAVE study is expected to be completed by end of 2024.
source: It is expected that a preliminary interim analysis on the efficacy of the PAVE strategy will be completed by the early 2024, and field recruitment will be completed by end of 2024.

claim: The efficacy phase is designed to assess the validity of the PAVE protocol by refining the AVE protocol using histopathology specimens and demonstrate the superiority of PAVE for detecting precancer and minimizing unnecessary referrals compared to the SOC.
source: The efficacy phase is designed to assess the validity of the PAVE protocol by refining the AVE protocol using histopathology specimens and demonstrate the superiority of PAVE for detecting precancer and minimizing unnecessary referrals compared to the SOC.

claim: The effectiveness phase is planned to examine additional factors including program feasibility, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness.
source: Following the initial efficacy phase, the effectiveness phase is planned to examine additional factors including program feasibility, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness.

claim: The Iris device will incorporate AI algorithms that aim to generate scores evaluating image quality, presence of precancerous lesions, and visibility of the SCJ based on digital cervix images.
source: The Iris device, used in PAVE, is an example of an AI-based system in healthcare. It will incorporate AI algorithms that aim to generate scores evaluating image quality, presence of precancerous lesions, and visibility of the SCJ based on digital cervix images.

claim: The AI algorithm used in the PAVE system can be considered an assistant to medical management offering the joint evaluation of the HPV data and the AVE outcome.
source: Considering its functionality, the AI algorithm used in the PAVE system, based on FDA specifications, can be considered an assistant to medical management offering the joint evaluation of the HPV data and the AVE outcome.
evidence: Based on inference about FDA specifications

claim: The selection of each device or assay in the PAVE strategy is based on factors such as accuracy to achieve its purpose and affordability.
source: The selection of each device or assay is based on factors such as accuracy to achieve its purpose (i.e. high sensitivity of the ScreenFire HPV test to detect precancer, high-quality image capture by the Iris device) and affordability.

claim: NCI PAVE collaborators have no commercial interests that could create appearance of conflict of interest.
source: It is important to note that NCI PAVE collaborators have no commercial interests that could create appearance of conflict of interest.

claim: De-implementation of existing strategies such as cytology, colposcopy, and VIA, as well as implementation of self-sampled HPV with AVE triage will require buy-in from stakeholders and policymakers as well as substantial investment in educating and retraining the laboratory and clinical workforces.
source: De-implementation of existing strategies, such as cytology, colposcopy, and VIA, as well as implementation of self-sampled HPV with AVE triage will require buy-in from stakeholders and policymakers as well as substantial investment in educating and retraining the laboratory and clinical workforces.
evidence: Based on inference about implementation challenges

claim: Cytology/colposcopy programs, though effective, are limited in scope and are costly to maintain.
source: Cytology/colposcopy programs, though effective, are limited in scope and are costly to maintain, therefore, switching may be attractive to health ministers.
evidence: Based on knowledge about existing screening programs

claim: The PAVE objective is to create an accurate, feasible, cost-effective screening and triage protocol for cervical cancer prevention in resource-limited settings.
source: The PAVE objective is to create an accurate, feasible, cost-effective screening and triage protocol for cervical cancer prevention in resource-limited settings.

claim: If proven effective, cost-effective, feasible, and acceptable, the PAVE strategy can have a major impact in reducing cervical cancer particularly among non-vaccinated adult women.
source: If proven effective, cost-effective, feasible, and acceptable, the strategy can have a major impact in reducing cervical cancer particularly among non-vaccinated adult women.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential impact

claim: The U.S. Cancer Moonshot initiative for Accelerated Control of Cervical Cancer has supported development of the new screening methods.
source: The U.S. Cancer Moonshot initiative for Accelerated Control of Cervical Cancer has supported development of the new screening methods (Perkins et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkins et al., 2023

claim: Projections were developed for approximately 65 low- and middle-income countries with age-standardized cervical cancer incidence greater than 10 per 100,000 women.
source: Projections were developed for the ~65 low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) with age-standardized cervical cancer incidence greater than 10 per 100,000 women (Perkins et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkins et al., 2023

claim: The projections conservatively assumed that screening and management would avert 25% of cervical cancer deaths beginning at age 50 years.
source: We conservatively and crudely assumed that screening and management would avert 25% of cervical cancer deaths (equivalent to screening uptake of 40% of eligible women, with 62.5% of screen-positive women receiving appropriate management) beginning at age 50 years.

claim: For vaccination cohorts, the projections assumed that a bivalent HPV16/18 vaccine with 90% uptake would avert 63% of cervical cancer deaths.
source: For vaccination cohorts, we assumed that a bivalent HPV16/18 vaccine (i.e. against the genotypes responsible for 70% of cervical cancers) with 90% uptake would avert 63% of cervical cancer deaths.

claim: A bivalent HPV16/18 vaccine targets genotypes responsible for 70% of cervical cancers.
source: For vaccination cohorts, we assumed that a bivalent HPV16/18 vaccine (i.e. against the genotypes responsible for 70% of cervical cancers) with 90% uptake would avert 63% of cervical cancer deaths.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about HPV vaccine coverage

claim: The projections assumed a single vaccine dose cost of US$4.50 with an average financial delivery cost per dose of US$7.
source: While data on the costs of implementing novel screening strategies and single-dose HPV vaccination for female adolescents are forthcoming from the HPV-automated visual evaluation (PAVE) consortium and single-dose vaccination studies, we crudely assumed a single vaccine dose cost US$4.5031 with an average financial delivery cost per dose (i.e. per fully immunized girl) of US$7 (Akumbom et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Akumbom et al., 2022

claim: The projections assumed a bundled financial cost per woman screened of US$15, including a low-cost rapid HPV genotyping assay with triage and treatment of screen-positive women.
source: We assumed a bundled financial cost per woman screened of US$15, including a low-cost rapid HPV genotyping assay with triage and treatment of screen-positive women.

claim: The cost per death averted for screening was US$4,400.
source: A one-time screening campaign for women aged 30–49 years in the selected countries yielded a financial cost of ~US$2.5 billion to avert ~570,000 deaths, or US$4,400 per death averted.

claim: The cost per death averted for vaccination was US$3,200.
source: On a similar order of magnitude, a one-time single-dose bivalent HPV vaccination campaign of girls aged 9–14 years in the same countries would cost ~US$2.0 billion and avert ~640,000 deaths, or US$3,200 per death averted.

claim: The ballpark estimates are undiscounted and do not account for cancer treatment cost offsets.
source: Of note, these ballpark estimates are undiscounted and do not account for cancer treatment cost offsets.

claim: The estimates did not consider demographic changes over the lifetime of intervention cohorts.
source: We also did not consider demographic changes over the lifetime of intervention cohorts, nor did we consider the indirect benefits of vaccination or prevention of other HPV-related cancers.

claim: The estimates did not consider the indirect benefits of vaccination or prevention of other HPV-related cancers.
source: We also did not consider demographic changes over the lifetime of intervention cohorts, nor did we consider the indirect benefits of vaccination or prevention of other HPV-related cancers.

claim: The PAVE study has two phases: efficacy (2023-2024) and effectiveness (planned to begin in 2024 or 2025).
source: The PAVE study has two phases: efficacy (2023–2024) and effectiveness (planned to begin in 2024 or 2025).

claim: The efficacy phase aims to refine and validate the screen-triage portion of the protocol.
source: The efficacy phase aims to refine and validate the screen-triage portion of the protocol.

claim: The effectiveness phase will research the introduction of the PAVE strategy into clinical practice.
source: The effectiveness phase will research the introduction of the PAVE strategy into clinical practice.

claim: Criteria for study site selection included existing screening programs, willingness to research self-sampled HPV for screening, capacity to run the HPV test, availability of pathology services to process biopsies, and access to treatment services including ablation, excision, and cancer treatment.
source: Criteria for study site selection included: (a) existing screening programs, (b) willingness to research self-sampled HPV for screening, (c) capacity to run the HPV test (d) availability of pathology services to process biopsies, and (e) access to treatment services including ablation, excision, and cancer treatment.

claim: The PAVE project is integrated into the screening activities at all study sites.
source: The PAVE project is integrated into the screening activities at all study sites, and at select sites is also integrated into other ongoing research studies.

claim: At select sites, the PAVE project is integrated into other ongoing research studies.
source: The PAVE project is integrated into the screening activities at all study sites, and at select sites is also integrated into other ongoing research studies.

claim: All ethical oversight of recruitment and clinical data collection will be done by the local sites under the guidance of their own Institutional Review Boards and will follow local guidelines.
source: All ethical oversight of recruitment and clinical data collection will be done by the local sites under the guidance of their own Institutional Review Boards and will follow local guidelines.

claim: All participants will have an informed consent for participation in the study and can drop their participation at any time during the process.
source: All participants will have an informed consent for participation in the study and can drop their participation at any time during the process.

claim: All study documents written in languages other than English are officially translated into English for study records.
source: All study documents written in languages other than English are officially translated into English for study records.

claim: Compiled analysis of de-identified data by NCI research staff for study purposes is deemed non-human subjects research by NIH.
source: Compiled analysis of de-identified data by NCI research staff for study purposes is deemed non-human subjects research by NIH.

claim: Self-samples (FLOQSwab) are delivered dry for testing.
source: Self-samples (FLOQSwab) are delivered dry for testing.

claim: HPV tests are run onsite or in local laboratories in a few days, with results returned to women quickly per local protocols.
source: HPV tests are run onsite or in local laboratories in a few days, with results returned to women quickly per local protocols.

claim: Women screening HPV-negative are informed of their results, reassured about their low subsequent risk of cervical cancer, and their participation in the study ends at most sites.
source: Women screening HPV-negative are informed of their results, reassured about their low subsequent risk of cervical cancer, and their participation in the study ends at most sites.

claim: Local clinicians record their VIA assessment (negative, positive, suspicion of cancer) or colposcopy impression (normal, low-grade, high-grade, or more severe).
source: Local clinicians also record their VIA assessment (negative, positive, suspicion of cancer) or colposcopy impression (normal, low-grade, high-grade, or more severe).

claim: HPV-positive women with a negative triage evaluation initially, but who are later identified by PAVE activities to have a precancer defined for study purposes as HPV-positive CIN2, CIN3 or AIS CIN2+, will be flagged and the clinical sites will be notified to permit 'safety net' recall for adequate management.
source: HPV-positive women with a negative triage evaluation initially, but who are later identified by PAVE activities to have a precancer defined for study purposes as HPV-positive CIN2, CIN3 or AIS CIN2+, will be flagged and the clinical sites will be notified to permit 'safety net' recall for adequate management.

claim: Study data including demographic survey information, HPV test results, VIA or colposcopy impression, and local pathology results are collected using District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2), Redcap or WEMA platforms.
source: Study data including demographic survey information, HPV test results (negative/positive, genotype for positive results), VIA or colposcopy impression, and local pathology results (cytology, biopsy, and/or excisional specimen) are collected using District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2), Redcap or WEMA platforms.

claim: All personal identification information is removed from datasets before transferring outside the country of origin.
